name: Hungry judge effect
statement: Israeli parole judges ruled for the prisoner in about 65% of cases at the start of a session and in almost none by its end.
meaning: The finding has a mechanism attached, and the mechanism is the contested part. Danziger, Levav and Avnaim-Pesso proposed that making one ruling after another depletes a judge's mental resources, and that a depleted judge falls back on the easier option. In a parole hearing the easier option is to deny, because denial preserves the status quo and takes less writing. A food break restores the resource and the grant rate jumps back. The popular version drops the mechanism and keeps the meal, which is how a paper about position in a queue became a paper about breakfast. What the authors measured was the ordinal position of a case within a session.

origin.who: Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav and Liora Avnaim-Pesso
origin.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Extraneous factors in judicial decisions" and opens by naming the caricature it sets out to test, that justice is what the judge ate for breakfast. It records the timing and length of two daily breaks, calls the morning one a snack of a sandwich and fruit served to the judge at the bench, and states that the data cannot test the breakfast claim directly.

evidence: 1,112 rulings by eight Jewish-Israeli judges sitting on two parole boards, collected over 50 days in a 10-month period. The boards handle about 40% of parole requests in the country. A judge heard 14 to 35 cases a day, an average of 22.58, each taking about six minutes. A morning snack and a lunch break split the day into three sessions, the first break falling after 7.8 cases on average and the second after 11.4. Overall 64.2% of requests were rejected, a figure that pools outright refusals with deferrals to a later hearing; deferrals are 48.4% of the reject category. The 65% and the near-zero endpoint are read off Figure 1 and repeated in the abstract, and no table in the paper prints them. That graph plots the proportion of favourable rulings against ordinal position, and is drawn from the first 95% of each session because the later positions hold few cases. A fixed-effects logistic regression controlling for offence severity, months served, previous imprisonments, rehabilitation programme, sex and ethnicity put the coefficient on the first decision of the third session at 2.873 (SE 0.425) and the coefficient on overall decision count at -0.078 (SE 0.020). Favourable rulings took longer than unfavourable ones, 7.37 minutes against 5.21, and their written verdicts ran 89.61 words against 47.36.

replication.headline: A large American arraignment court shows a decline of about 6 percentage points across a session and no rise after the meal break, and an Arkansas traffic court shows a decline in arraignments but not in trials.
replication.detail: The dispute runs in three separate arguments. Weinshall-Margel and Shapard interviewed three attorneys, a parole panel judge and five prison service and court staff, and reported that case order is not random: a board tries to finish one prison before breaking and to start another after, and unrepresented prisoners usually go last. In their own 227 decisions from 12 hearing days, unrepresented prisoners were about a third of cases and prevailed 15% of the time against 35% for those with counsel. Dropping deferrals from the original data, they put the within-session slide at about 75% falling to 42% rather than 65% falling to zero. Danziger and colleagues replied that they added legal representation to every model and reran it, that case order and the meal break stayed robust predictors, and that on the five days where they know the prison of origin, prisoners from the same prison appear both before and after a break. They did not report how much the effect shrank. Glöckner attacked the magnitude. A drop from 65% to 5% is an odds ratio of 35, or d = 1.96, which he sets against a publication-bias-corrected meta-analytic estimate for mental depletion of d = -0.10 to 0.25 and a 23-lab registered replication he cites at d = 0.04. He then simulated an unbiased judge who declines to start a case she cannot finish before the break, using the ruling times the original paper reports, and produced a curve of similar shape from a 36% base rate. Censoring the last 5% of each session, as the original graph does, deepened the simulated drop and produced one even when the simulated judge had no foresight. He put the drop such a judge would generate at 15% to 45%, so his claim is that the effect is overstated rather than absent. The field test is Shroff and Vamvourellis, who examined 96,318 pretrial arraignments by 41 judges in a large urban American court system between 2010 and 2015. Covariate-adjusted release rates fell about 6 percentage points across the hours before lunch and before dinner, stayed flat through the sessions after them, and did not rise once judges had eaten. Hemrajani and Hobert found charges less likely to be dismissed late in a session in Pulaski County traffic arraignments in 2019 and 2020, and no such pattern in trial hearings in the same court. Their abstract reports no test of a rebound after a break.

study.cite: Shroff, R., & Vamvourellis, K. (2022). Pretrial release judgments and decision fatigue. Judgment and Decision Making, 17(6), 1176-1207.

limits: This search found no repeat of the Israeli analysis on fresh Israeli parole data. Glöckner records that the data were not available to him, the authors being willing to share but blocked by those who first gave them access, so his critique simulates the process instead of reanalysing it. Daljord, Urminsky and Ureta thank Levav for the data, and their reanalysis is still a preprint rather than a peer-reviewed paper; it does not dispute the cyclical pattern and argues that the status quo account of depletion does not fit it. The two field studies are not replications in the strict sense, because American pretrial arraignment and Arkansas traffic court differ from Israeli parole in stakes, in who controls the order and in what the default ruling is. Shroff and Vamvourellis do find a decline within a session, so their result is not a flat null. What they fail to find is the part that carries the depletion account, the rebound after eating.
misreadings: The paper does not record what any judge ate for breakfast, and it says its data cannot test the breakfast claim directly. What it records of the meals is the timing and length of the two breaks and a sandwich and fruit at the morning one. What it tested was position in a sequence. The near-zero endpoint is the tail of a plotted curve whose later positions hold few cases, not a finding that late applicants never win. Deferral to a later hearing is counted with rejection, which the authors defend as psychologically equivalent and Weinshall-Margel and Shapard reject as legally distinct. The critics also disagree with each other, and flattening them into one verdict misreports all three. Weinshall-Margel and Shapard call the post-break peak an artifact of case ordering. Glöckner argues the effect is overstated rather than absent, and says his account leaves parts of the pattern unexplained. Chatziathanasiou goes furthest, concluding that the correlation was spurious and that there is no hungry judge effect.
